clue.text: Would one toast their success at work?

definitions.text: Would one toast their success at work?

parts.words: Would one toast their success at work?
parts.note: read as raising a glass to doing well in a job, but really people who earn the loaf by working might grill what they have won

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone would drink to their own professional triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toast' suggests drinking a toast; the second reading is grilling the bread you have won by working.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who earn the family income are proverbially said to win the household's loaf.

clue.text: Prime minister who was kidnapped

definitions.meaning: David, hero of Stevenson's novel Kidnapped, has this surname

explanation.surface: Recalling a premier who was abducted.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Louis Stevenson's Kidnapped features young David Balfour; Arthur Balfour was a British prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a Conservative premier and the surname of Stevenson's abducted hero.

clue.text: In the outcome, I would get clear

indicators.note: In tells us one piece goes inside another

parts.note: an event can mean an outcome, as in 'in the event'
I'd is the contraction of I would

explanation.surface: Someone expects to get a clear result in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obvious or plain to see is clear.

clue.text: Identify smack one's picked up in an estuary

indicators.note: in tells us to put the turned pieces inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river with a broad estuary between England and Wales

indicators.note: in a down clue picked up means read upwards, so the pieces are reversed

parts.note: a smack is a taste or flavour, a tang
one's is one is, giving I and S

explanation.surface: Spotting a fishing smack collected in an estuary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a fishing boat, apt beside the estuary; here it is a taste. 'picked up' turns the pieces to read SIGNAT, which goes inside the river.
explanation.definitionFit: To designate is to name or specify something, so to identify it.

clue.text: Singer has form of savings account

parts.note: an ISA is an Individual Savings Account, a British tax-free savings scheme

explanation.surface: A vocalist has a particular type of savings account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is not a vocalist but a surname: Isaac Bashevis Singer the novelist, or Isaac Singer of sewing machines.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Bashevis Singer won the Nobel Prize for Literature; it is his first name.

clue.text: Making observation about hearts being for love

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the letter

parts.note: noting is making an observation
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

explanation.surface: Remarking that playing hearts is all about love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love' as in tennis scoring means zero.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis scoring, love means zero, a score of none.

clue.text: Dance band half refused sort of tipsy-cake

parts.note: the rumba is a Cuban dance

indicators.note: half of the word band is refused, kept out, leaving only its first half

explanation.surface: A dance band where half the musicians decline a boozy pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half refused' drops ND from BAND, keeping BA. A rum baba is a yeast cake soaked in rum syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small sponge soaked in rum syrup, a kind of tipsy cake.

clue.text: Haul German over to endure cane

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above, so these come before the next piece

parts.note: swag is a haul of stolen goods
to stick something is to endure it

explanation.surface: Dragging a German along to suffer a beating with a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haul' is a noun, loot, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A short cane carried by military officers is this kind of stick.

clue.text: Micawber succeeds? About the same

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word is placed around the other

parts.note: to succeed is to triumph, so succeeds gives wins
ilk means the same kind, as in 'of that ilk'

explanation.surface: Asking whether Dickens's optimist ever actually prospers, and answering that it's always the same story.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield, ever hopeful that something will turn up, has this first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's character Mr Micawber in David Copperfield bears this as his first name.

clue.text: Head-hunter's technique is to get me back in

indicators.note: in tells us to place one piece inside the other two joined together

parts.note: art is skill or technique
taken as written

indicators.note: back means the word me is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A recruitment consultant explains their method is to get the speaker back into a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head-hunter' looks like a recruiter, but means the chief huntress among the Greek gods.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of hunting is the foremost huntress of the Olympian pantheon.

clue.text: Chop all wands into pieces in show of disapproval

indicators.note: into pieces suggests breaking up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A magician's wands are chopped up, to the audience's displeasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into pieces' rearranges CHOPALLWANDS.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience's slow rhythmic clapping signals impatience or contempt.

clue.text: Thank heavens, bishop luckier than curate in this?

definitions.text: Thank heavens, bishop luckier than curate in this?

parts.words: Thank heavens, bishop luckier than curate in this?
parts.note: alludes to the Punch cartoon where a curate, served a bad breakfast, says it is good in parts; the bishop's would be wholly sound, and the phrase is also an old exclamation of approval

explanation.surface: A churchman's relief that the bishop fared better than his junior colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: In the famous Punch cartoon a curate, given a stale breakfast by his bishop, says it is 'good in parts'; the bishop presumably got a sound one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated British exclamation of approval, and literally a fresh breakfast item, unlike the curate's.

clue.text: Marx touring a grand city

indicators.note: touring means going round, so one piece surrounds the others

parts.note: Chico was one of the Marx Brothers
G is short for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: One of the Marx Brothers on tour in a fine metropolis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' looks like an adjective for the city; it is G, slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Illinois metropolis on Lake Michigan is a major American city.

clue.text: One European to the fore in welcome for one with plume

indicators.note: to the fore means brought to the front, so a letter moves to the start

parts.note: to welcome someone is to greet them
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A ceremonial greeting led by a single European wearing a feather.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the two Es in GREET moves to the front, leaving E+GRET.
explanation.definitionFit: This heron is noted for the long ornamental breeding feathers once prized for hats.

clue.text: Diagram of car, a collector's item perhaps

parts.note: auto is short for automobile, a car
a graph is a diagram plotting data

explanation.surface: A drawing of a vehicle that might become a collectable.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the diagram first, but the car comes first in the answer, with 'of' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrity's signature is a typical item sought by collectors.

clue.text: Happen to choose serving of fish, say

parts.note: to take is to choose, as in take your pick

indicators.note: say signals the word is spoken, giving a similar-sounding spelling

parts.note: plaice is a flatfish commonly served

explanation.surface: Choosing a portion of fish for dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: When an event occurs it is said to occur in a given place.

clue.text: From impromptu inspection, see something to announce to board opponent?

parts.note: to spot something is to see it

parts.words: something to announce to board opponent
parts.note: in chess you announce check to your opponent when threatening their king

explanation.surface: A surprise inspection reveals something a player should tell their chess rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is the chessboard, not a company board.
explanation.definitionFit: An unannounced random examination is a standard term for a surprise test or inspection.

clue.text: Old guard accepting fine for misdemeanour

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a fence is a barrier that guards
F is the abbreviation for fine, on pencils

explanation.surface: An elderly security guard taking a fine for a minor crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' looks like a penalty, which suits a misdemeanour, but it is just the pencil-grade letter; it sits right after the guard's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor crime or wrongdoing is a breach of the law.

clue.text: Not much volume to sound in Monteverdi

parts.note: CL is a centilitre, a small measure of volume
audio means sound

explanation.surface: A complaint that a Monteverdi recording is too quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'volume' suggests loudness, but it is a liquid measure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer Monteverdi's first name is this.

clue.text: Puttin' on wig, etc, to give bird

indicators.note: the clue's own dropped-g spelling of the first word tells us to clip the final g off the word that follows in the same way

parts.note: getting on a wig, gown and the like is robing, as a judge does

explanation.surface: A judge getting dressed in wig and gown ends up giving us a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase reads as 'robin'', a judge's dressing in wig and gown with the final G dropped as in 'Puttin''; 'to give' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-breasted songbird is a familiar garden bird.

clue.text: Fail to maintain progress in run: get moving, please

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for run in cricket

indicators.note: get moving suggests stirring up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A coach urges a runner to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get moving' rearranges PLEASE to ELAPSE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To slip back into a former worse state is to fail to keep improving.

clue.text: Boss getting aboard club's small boat

indicators.note: getting aboard means going inside, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: a bat is a club
an umbo is the boss in the centre of a shield

explanation.surface: The chief boards the club's dinghy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is not the chief but UMBO, the raised centre of a shield. A bumboat sells provisions to ships at anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: A small vessel ferrying goods to ships lying offshore.

clue.text: Be provocative, wearing feminine dress material

parts.note: if you are wearing clothes you are in them
lamé is a fabric woven with metallic thread

explanation.surface: Wearing a feminine dress of shiny fabric to stir things up.
explanation.walkthrough: LAMÉ is a glittering fabric with metallic threads.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir up anger or passion is to act in a provoking way.

clue.text: Tourist mass encountered, going to one end of England

indicators.note: going to here means heading the answer, placed at the front
one end of picks the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: met means encountered

explanation.surface: A mass of tourists met, travelling to one end of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cornwall an emmet is a tourist, from the dialect word for ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornish dialect calls holidaymakers by this word meaning ant.

clue.text: Compile shocking attack

indicators.note: shocking suggests something badly disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Gathering together a damning assault on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shocking' rearranges COMPILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A strongly worded written or spoken assault on someone's views is a classic piece of invective.

clue.text: State in which we are all united?

definitions.text: State in which we are all united?

parts.words: State in which we are all united?
parts.note: sounds like a utopian condition of harmony, but refers to the British nation whose name begins with United

explanation.surface: A dream of a country where everyone lives in harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: The UK is the United Kingdom, so its citizens live in a realm with united in its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm ruled by a monarch is a state, as in the United one.

clue.text: Handled ancient Greek vessel

parts.note: reads as a ship someone steered, but means a jar with handles used in classical Greece

explanation.surface: Someone steered a ship of the ancient Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handled' looks like a verb for steering a ship; it is an adjective, having handles, and the vessel is a jar.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-handled storage jar for wine or oil was common in classical Greece.

clue.text: Not fair to describe part of Orion thus?

definitions.meaning: unfair, as a boxing blow too low

definitions.text: to describe part of Orion thus?
definitions.meaning: the constellation Orion has a famous belt of three stars, with his sword hanging beneath it

explanation.surface: Questioning whether it is fair to describe a bit of a constellation this way.
explanation.walkthrough: In boxing a punch below the waistband is illegal; Orion's sword hangs beneath his three-star belt.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing foul for a low punch, hence any unfair remark or tactic.
